'''Amelia Reid''' (November 13, 1924 – March 3, 2001) was a mathematician, pilot, [[flight instructor]], businesswoman, [[airshow]] performer, and airport advocate. She was the founder of Amelia Reid Aviation (now AeroDynamic Aviation) and is known as California's First Lady of Aviation.<ref name="AOPA" />

== Early life and education ==
Reid got her first taste of flying in 1940 when pilot [[Evelyn Sharp (aviator)|Evelyn Sharp]] took her on a ride in a Piper Cub J-2.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Donnelly |first=Kathleen |date=1993-03-14 |title=AFTER 50 YEARS, FLIGHT STILL SUITS HER FANCY |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-1993-03-14-9303191987-story.html |access-date=2023-12-03 |website=Chicago Tribune}}</ref> In 1941 Reid had her first flying lessons,<ref name="AOPA" /> and in May 1946 she earned her pilot's license.<ref name=":1" />
[[File:Amelia Reid plaque.jpg|thumb|A plaque honoring Reid at Reid Hillview Airport in [[San Jose, California|San Jose]].]]

Reid studied mathematics at [[University of Nebraska at Kearney|Kearney State College]] in Nebraska, earning her bachelor's degree in June 1945.<ref name="AOPA" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" /> Reid then attended [[San Jose State University]] where she earned her master's degree in mathematics.<ref name="AOPA" /> She worked at [[NACA]] (now known as [[NASA]]) as a [[Computer (occupation)|human computer]] and [[Programmer|programing mathematician]] from 1945 to 1958.<ref name="AOPA" /><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Ngaotheppitak |first=Ratana |date=November 2010 |title=Guide to the Amelia Reid National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA) Human Computer Papers, 1945–1958 |url=https://oac.cdlib.org/findaid/ark:/13030/kt4q2nf1p4/entire_text/ |access-date=2023-12-02 |website=oac.cdlib.org}}</ref> Because the NACA [[Ames Research Center]], where she worked, did not allow flexibility in her work schedule, she left after the birth of her son.<ref name="AOPA" />

==Career==

From there Reid returned to flying and became a certified commercial pilot with instructor ratings in 1960.<ref name="AOPA" /> That same year, Reid founded Amelia Reid Aviation, a flight school at [[Reid-Hillview Airport]] in [[San Jose, California|San Jose]], California.<ref name="AOPA" />  The company bought their first aircraft, a Taylorcraft L-2, for just $350. Reid initially ran the business out of her 1959 Ford and, later, out of two trailers.<ref name=":1" /> She mortgaged her home and constructed a permanent [[hangar]] and office building in 1967, from which she operated her flight school for the rest of her life.<ref name="Merc" /><ref name=":1" />

Reid logged over 55,000 flight hours and trained more than 4,000 pilots.<ref name="AOPA" /> She flew in countless [[airshows]], her last at age 75 in a [[Cessna 150|Cessna Aerobat]]. She won the 1996 [[Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association]] Lawrence P. Sharples Award and was inducted into the [[National Association of Flight Instructors]] Hall of Fame.<ref name="Merc">{{cite news |last=Sweeney |first=Frank |date=March 5, 2001 |title=Top San Jose flight instructor Amelia Reid dies |work=The San Jose Mercury News |url=http://archives.californiaaviation.org/ganews/msg09478.html |url-status=dead |access-date=2009-05-06 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304103314/http://archives.californiaaviation.org/ganews/msg09478.html |archive-date=March 4, 2016}}</ref><ref name="AOPA">{{cite web |last=AOPA Communications staff |date=March 5, 2001 |title=Aviation community mourns Amelia Reid, California's 'First Lady of General Aviation' and AOPA Sharples Award winner |url=http://www.aopa.org/whatsnew/newsitems/2001/01-1-076.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090407051536/http://www.aopa.org/whatsnew/newsitems/2001/01-1-076.html |archive-date=7 April 2009 |access-date=2009-05-06 |website=AOPA Online |publisher=Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association}}</ref><ref name="NAFI">{{cite web|url=http://nafinet.org/programs/hof_list.html|title=Flight Instructors Hall of Fame Inductees|year=2007|publisher=National Association of Flight Instructors|access-date=2009-05-06}}</ref>

Reid's students include noted airshow performer [[Sean D. Tucker]],<ref name="AOPA" /> aviation author and speaker [[Rod Machado]], aerospace engineer and author [[H. Paul Shuch]] (whose recurring fictional character Avalon Eden<ref name="Avalon Eden">{{cite web |title=The Avalon Eden Stories |url=http://avsport.org/publicat/index.html#avalon |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091024030753/http://nafinet.org/programs/hof_list.html |archive-date=2009-10-24 |access-date=2013-05-26 |website=AvSport of Lock Haven}}</ref> is based in part on Reid), and Jason Dahl, the captain on [[United Airlines Flight 93|United flight 93]] on [[September 11, 2001]].

== Activism ==
In the 1960s, [[Reid–Hillview Airport|Reid-Hillview Airport]], founded in 1939 by five local airmen including Reid's father-in-law, was sold to [[Santa Clara County, California|Santa Clara County]].<ref name="AOPA" /> The growth of [[Silicon Valley]] in the San Jose area instigated campaigns to close the airport.<ref name="AOPA" /> Reid was a strong advocate of the preservation of the airport and a founder of the Reid-Hillview Airport Association.

==Later life==

On January 16, 2001, Reid had a stroke, and she died on March 3, 2001, at age 76.<ref name="AOPA" />
